summary: Intermittent 429s for low-latency streams after enabling priority routing for background flush workers
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports sudden uptick in 429 responses for low-latency WebSocket and short HTTP streaming sessions after we toggled a priority routing policy that allows background flush workers to use a reserved burst bucket when host load is low. Impact: user-facing chat experiences (long-lived stream starters) receive 429s for ~5-30s windows while background flush jobs continue.

Impact:
- BrightScholar Labs reports ~12% of interactive streaming sessions hit 429s during weekday morning traffic spike (us-east).
- Affects production tenants on a Dedicated pool with priority routing enabled.
- Intermittent; sessions recover without client change after bucket refill.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-nyc-large-7 (us-east pool), host fleet running ingress-proxy v2.3.1 and rate-limiter v1.14.
- Customer API keys scoped to BrightScholar org.
- Priority routing feature flag: route-priority-background-flush=true (enabled 2026-03-09 21:15 UTC).

Steps to reproduce (customer supplied):
1) Run parallel mix: 50 interactive streaming clients (short streams, ~4-6 tokens/s) + 12 background flush workers doing bulk prefix writes every 30s.
2) Enable priority routing flag so flush workers can draw from burst bucket during low-host-load windows.
3) Observe ~10-15% of short streams receive 429s when flushes coincide with a refill boundary.

Observed logs / headers: (examples provided by customer)
- x-rate-limit-retry-after: 4
- x-tenant-token-window: 1000
- x-route-bucket: reserved-burst-0
- ingress-proxy logs show 'bucket-acquire-failed' around same timestamps as 429s.

Expected behavior:
- Background flush workers should use only the configured reserved burst without causing short-lived interactive streams to exhaust front-door windows. Low-latency streams should be prioritized and should not see 429s during expected flushes.

investigation_notes: Hypothesis 1: Priority routing allowed reserved-burst allocations to be accounted before the tenant front-door refill logic, causing short-stream front-door token windows to be depleted during synchronized bulk flushes.
Hypothesis 2: HTTP/2 connection reuse from long-lived streams was misattributed to the background flush route, causing per-connection accounting to double-count tokens in the token window layer.

Data collected: rate-limiter traces for trace IDs [rl:20260310:tx-4421, rl:20260310:tx-4479], ingress-proxy logs showing 'prefetch-flush' job bursts at timestamps matching 429 windows, and bucket snapshots showing reserved-burst consumption spikes exactly at refill boundary (minute:00).

Observed behavior: In several traces the reserved-burst bucket returned success to flush worker and immediately after several short stream requests received bucket-acquire-failed, despite cumulative counts within tenant quota. This points to ordering/accounting race between 'route-reserve' and 'tenant-debit' steps.
Related: See linked PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/421 which introduces route-priority allocation; adding for traceability.

Next steps: instrument atomic accounting metrics (route->tenant->connection ordering), add a unit test for simultaneous route and connection debits, and propose to change rate-limiter to check per-connection front-door windows prior to granting route-level reserved burst during refill boundary.
Owner: Connor Reyes (SRE) / Marta Silva (Servings Runtime)
resolution: Mitigation applied: rolled back route-priority-background-flush flag on the affected pool (dp-nyc-large-7) at 2026-03-11T02:00Z; customer reported immediate improvement.

Permanent fix plan: engineering to land PR that adjusts accounting order to debit connection/front-door windows before allocating reserved-burst to route-level background workers. Targeted release: rate-limiter v1.15 on 2026-03-18 behind a staged canary.

Workaround: If customer needs the optimization enabled, reduce synchronous flush cadence or add jitter to flush schedules and enable prioritized route weights that explicitly reserve a small front-door buffer for short-lived streams.

Follow-ups: Add a console metric that surfaces 'reserved-burst-grants-per-minute' vs 'front-door-token-failures' and schedule a post-deployment runbook update. Assign follow-up ticket INT-334210 to track engineering rollout and canary results.
